In this paper, we present a comprehensive performance evaluation of deep learning networks for semantic segmentation of traffic stereo-pair images. We explore the use of various deep learning architectures, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), for semantic segmentation of traffic scenes from stereo-pair images. We evaluate the performance of these networks using a large dataset of stereo-pair images captured from various traffic scenarios, and compare their performance using different evaluation metrics. Our results show that CNNs outperform RNNs in terms of segmentation accuracy, with the best-performing CNN achieving an accuracy of 93.6%. We also analyze the effect of different parameters, such as image resolution, batch size, and number of epochs, on the segmentation performance. Our results indicate that increasing the image resolution and batch size improves segmentation accuracy, while increasing the number of epochs has a diminishing effect on performance. 

We also perform a thorough analysis of the segmentation results, including a class-wise analysis of the errors and a study of the impact of different object classes on the overall segmentation accuracy. 

Our results show that the CNNs struggle with certain object classes, such as pedestrians and motorcycles, and that improving the segmentation accuracy of these classes is crucial for achieving high overall segmentation accuracy. 

Our findings have important implications for the development of autonomous driving systems, which rely heavily on accurate semantic segmentation of traffic scenes. 

We demonstrate that deep learning networks can achieve high segmentation accuracy on stereo-pair images, but that further research is needed to improve the accuracy of certain object classes. 

Our results also highlight the importance of carefully selecting the appropriate deep learning architecture, hyperparameters, and evaluation metrics for semantic segmentation tasks. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive evaluation of deep learning networks for semantic segmentation of traffic stereo-pair images, and provides valuable insights for the development of autonomous driving systems.

> We study some properties of multi-letter quantum finite automata (QFA) and their relation to classical ones, in particular we show that every QFA with $n$ input letters can be simulated by equivalent one with only two input letters. This result generalizes previous work done by Kondacs et al., where it was shown that any single letter QFA can be simulated by another one using at most three input letters. In addition, we prove that there exists universal QFA which accepts all languages accepted by QFAs with $k$ input letters, for each fixed $k$. Finally, we give a characterization of the class of regular languages recognized by QFAs with $k$ input letters, as well as description of the structure of such machines.

In this paper, we propose novel approach for electron microscopy image segmentation using a semi-supervised hierarchical merge tree (SSHMT) algorithm. Electron microscopy images are highly complex and require accurate segmentation for feature extraction and analysis. However, obtaining annotated data for supervised learning is challenging due to the time-consuming and labor-intensive nature of manual annotation.

To address this challenge, we propose SSHMT, which leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to learn a hierarchical representation of image. The proposed method consists of two main components: semi-supervised learning framework that learns a hierarchy of features from labeled data, and merge tree that combines features from different levels of hierarchy to segment the image.

The semi-supervised learning framework is based on a deep neural network that takes both labeled and unlabeled data as input. The network learns to predict the labels for labeled data and simultaneously learns representation of unlabeled data. The learned representation is then used to construct hierarchy of features by clustering similar features together.

The merge tree is novel data structure that enables efficient and effective segmentation of image. The tree is constructed by recursively partitioning the image into smaller regions based on the similarity of the features. Each node in tree represents region of the image, and the leaf nodes correspond to smallest regions that can be segmented. The merge tree allows for efficient propagation of labels from labeled data to unlabeled data, enabling accurate segmentation of the entire image.

We evaluate performance of SSHMT on several electron microscopy datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art segmentation methods. The results show that SSHMT outperforms the compared methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of SSHMT in segmenting large-scale electron microscopy images, which is a significant challenge in the field.

In summary, SSHMT is a novel approach for electron microscopy image segmentation that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to learn a hierarchical representation of the image. The

The Schwinger holographic effect is the generation of electric charges by quantum mechanics in a strongly interacting system. We explore the rotation of a probe D3-brane in an AdS5 x S5 configuration representing N=4 super Yang–Mills theory at strong coupling. The rotation of the brane is accompanied by a generation of new charges. This leads to an understanding of the influence of angular momentum on the generation of charges in the Schwinger holographic effect. This may be of significance in high energy physics applications involving rapidly spinning objects like neutron stars and black holes.

analyzing 3D clinical pictures is a challenging and difficult task in clinical imagery research. Recently, self-supervised learning (SSL) has demonstrated remarkable promise in studying 3D image representations without expensive manual labels. Moreover, existing SSL techniques are often limited to weak 3D shape priors, which can lead to inconsistent performance. In this paper, we propose a Prior-Guided Local Self-supervised Language (PGL) approach that can successfully leverage strong 3D anatomical shape priors for better 3D medical image segmentation. PGL consists of three fundamental elements: (1) a local self-supervised learning module that can develop robust 3D image representations by creating 3D patches with various shapes and orientations; and (2) a global prior-guided module that can regularize the learned 3D image representations by adding 3D shape priors. We evaluate the proposed PGL method on three public 3D medical image segmentation datasets, i.e., the Body Brain Segmentation (BraTS) data and the Multimodal Body Tumor Segmentation (BRATS) data. Experimental findings show that our PGL approach can greatly reduce the efficiency of 3D medical image segmentation compared to state-of-the-art SSL techniques.

The puiseux characteristic of a Goursat germ is a measure of the number of branches Emanating from the germ At each point. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive study of the Puiseux characteristic for Goursat germs. We begin by Introducing the basic definitions and properties of Goursat germs. Next, we establish the Puiseux characteristic of Goursat germs and provide a rigorous proof of its properties. We also discuss the relationship between the Puiseux characteristic and other important properties of Goursat germs, such as the versal deformations and the geometric monodromy. Finally, we demonstrate the practical applications of the Puiseux characteristic in various fields of mathematics, including singularity theory and Algebraic geometry. Our results Contribute to a better understanding of the structure and behavior of Goursat germs and provide valuable insights for future research in this area.

We study the extreme properties of two game theoretic models, one based on Flooding Game and other on Prisoner's Dilemma. We find that both models exhibit interesting property known as 'extremality', which we term 'extreme extremity'. Extreme extremity arises when the probability of winning in a given game depends on outcome of previous games. In particular, it occurs when the expected value of winning in a given game depends on outcomes of all previous games. This result has important implications for understanding the dynamics of cooperation and competition in social dilemmas.

In this paper, we propose LadderNet, a novel deep learning architecture for medical image segmentation. LadderNet is based on the U-Net design and consists of different paths with multiple dilation rates. This study presents novel approach to liver segmentation in abdominal computed tomography (CT) images using an auto-context neural network with self-supervised contour attention. The proposed method utilizes contextual information from neighboring slices to improve accuracy, while contour attention module focuses on enhancing boundary detection of the liver. Experimental results demonstrate that our technique outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving high Dice similarity coefficients and demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately segmenting the liver in CT scans. This innovative methodology has significant potential for improving automated analysis of medical imaging data.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to semantic segmentation in pathology using an adaptive weighting multi-field-of-view convolutional neural network (CNN). Current state-of-the-art methods for semantic segmentation in pathology are limited by their reliance on a single field of view (FOV), which can result in reduced accuracy due to the varying sizes and orientations of histopathological samples. To address this limitation, we introduce an adaptive weighting mechanism that allows our model to dynamically adjust the importance of different FOVs based on their relevance to the current sample.

Our proposed method consists of three main components: (1) a multi-FOV dataset generation module, which creates a set of images with different FOVs from a single slide; (2) a feature extraction module, which extracts features from each image in the dataset using a pre-trained CNN; and (3) a classification module, which uses the extracted features to predict the class label for each image. The key innovation of our approach is the use of an adaptive weighting scheme, which assigns weights to each FOV based on its similarity to the current sample. This allows our model to selectively focus on the most relevant FOVs, improving overall accuracy and reducing the impact of irrelevant information.

We evaluate our method on two publicly available datasets and compare it to several state-of-the-art approaches. Our results show that our adaptive weighting multi-FOV CNN outperforms existing methods, achieving an average increase in accuracy of 10% across all classes. Additionally, we perform a series of ablation studies to analyse the effectiveness of our adaptive weighting mechanism, demonstrating that it significantly improves performance compared to fixed weighting schemes.

Overall, our work presents a significant advancement in the field of semantic segmentation in pathology, providing a more accurate and robust approach to tackling the challenges posed by variable-size histopathological samples. The proposed method has important implications for clinical applications, where accurate segmentation can improve diagnosis and treatment of diseases.

This paper explores the Ott-Antonnesen (OA) attractiveness for parametre-dependent oscillatory networks, a concept crucial in understanding interconnected oscillators' collective dynamical behaviours, including synchrony or incoherence. Although OA theory is usually applied to systems with a fixed parametre set, we investigate its relevance for parametre-dependent networks involving complex topologies and interactions. Theoretical and numerical studies of Kuramoto-Sakaguchi oscillators with varied coupling strengths and natural frequencies were performed, uncovering a broad parametre range where OA attractiveness holds. Our findings present a significant expansion of the known applicability of OA theory and provide new insights into the broader universality class of attractors in machinery and biological oscillatory networks.

This contribution considers learning to steer using hidden unit networks as described in our prior work, which demonstrated efficacy when incorporating nonlinearities in both feature extraction and loss propagation along with simple learning rules. Our next step was to see it executed on large-scale task space—the entire Internet. Instead of training manually, we adapted algorithms from some well-known distributed control simulations at a stately AI lab, where they successfully completed more than 700 hours of training. We trained small groups of units that were explicitly coded to perform tasks such as auto tracking or steering maneuvers via three dimensions of features from auxiliary neural network networks (ANNs), namely k 1,k 2,…, k N. The feature vectors are constructed by drawing an image in each row of 2x2 grids on top of which various numbers of 3 dimensional arrays lie. After initializing some parameters, ANNs represent their inputs and outputs and learn how to predict values from these arrays as the number of columns in each dimension increases. However, there appears to be inherent problem that arises, at least with regard to steering operations; we describe here two solutions to this challenge, namely learning to steer through iterative adaptive control simulations. We illustrate them in detail first on first task involving manual driving. Then, we take situation one step further by extending similar techniques to support navigation at scale—using tensorflow—including scenarios such as multi-user games, robot controlled vehicles, etc. In conclusion, we emphasize that learning to steer can lead engineers to make decisions faster and safer because it improves overall performance while maintaining flexibility enough to achieve the right balance between accuracy versus flexibility.

Many applications in digital signal processing require the use of matrices with good peak-to-sidelobe ratios (PSRs). 

For instance, PSR-optimal matching pursuit has been shown to outperform conventional matching pursuit in terms of reconstruction quality. However, the design of matrices with good PSRs is a challenging problem. In this paper, we propose a novel method for constructing binary matrices with good PSRs based on an experimental approach. We first generate a set of binary matrices with randomly chosen row and column weights. 

We then select the matrix with the best PSR from this set, and use it as the starting point for our construction. 

We iteratively modify the selected matrix by adding or removing rows and columns, with the aim of improving its PSR. 

We show that our method is able to generate binary matrices with PSRs that are significantly better than those of randomly generated matrices. Furthermore, we compare the performance of our method with that of other state-of-the-art methods, and show that our method outperforms these methods in terms of PSR.

We claim that the Monty Hall problem is not a probability puzzle but rather a challenge in mathematical modelling. By mathematical modelling we mean the following: given a problem with uncertain, complicated truth, find a model that captures salient features of the truth, is simple to work with, and yields predictions that are accurate in practice. Consider the variant of the Monty Hall problem in which a contestant faces three doors, one with a car and two with goats. The contestant chooses a door. Then the host, who knows where the car is, opens one of the goat doors. He then asks the contestant if she wants to switch her choice to the remaining closed door. Mathematicians have long agreed that the contestant should switch doors. But confront a freind with the problem and ask her to solve it, and it is unlikely that she will arrive at the correct answer. In forming an intuition for the problem, people seem to fall into two groups. One group, like me, is inevitably confused by the problem, and fails to see the obvious answer. The other group, like my collaegue Gary Miller, sees the answer imediately. Who is right? Given the inherent uncertainty in modelling human cognition, both groups could be right. The group that switches doors may well be making the optimal decision, since it has embraced a model that renders the best predictions about the true outcome. In a sense, the problem is not about probability at all, but about modelling human cognition and the inherent uncertainty in that modelling. If so, there is no longer an issue to debate. This paper explores these ideas, leading to the conclusion that there is no longer a contraversy about the Monty Hall problem. The contraversy is resolved, not by logic, but by embracing modelling uncertainty.

Abstract: Holistic decomposition convolution (HDC) is a novel method for efficient semantic segmentation of 3D MR images. HDC uses locally-decimated Convolutional Neural Systems (CNNs) with a 3D MR imagery segmentation algorithm to obtain precise and reliable segmentation. The proposed technique uses a sparse convolutional layer to capture regional context and a dense convolutional layer to capture regional details. The sparse layer provides a novel holistically-decomposed convolutional filter that allows the network to accurately capture the global context of the input image. The dense layer uses a standard convolutional filter to capture local details. The proposed technique has been implemented on the MRI segmentation challenge 2017 dataset and achieved competitive results compared to other state-of-the-art approaches.

In this paper, we explore the use of uncertainty estimation in deep learning segmentation of fluorescence microscopy images with missing markers. Fluorescence microscopy is a widely used technique in biology and medicine, which allows for the visualization of specific biological structures or molecules of interest through the use of fluorescent dyes. However, the accuracy of the segmentation process can be hindered by the absence of markers, which can lead to incorrect classification of pixels and reduced accuracy in downstream analysis.

To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that leverages uncertainty estimation in deep learning to improve the segmentation of fluorescence microscopy images with missing markers. Our approach uses a Bayesian neural network to learn the posterior distribution over the class labels and uncertainty of each pixel, allowing us to quantify the uncertainty in the segmentation process. We evaluate our approach on a dataset of fluorescence microscopy images with missing markers and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving segmentation accuracy compared to traditional deep learning segmentation methods.

Our results show that our approach is able to accurately segment fluorescence microscopy images with missing markers, outperforming traditional deep learning methods. We also demonstrate the utility of the uncertainty estimates in identifying regions of high uncertainty, which can be used to guide manual annotation or further experimental validation.

Our work has important implications for the analysis of fluorescence microscopy images in biology and medicine, particularly in situations where markers are not available or are difficult to detect. By leveraging uncertainty estimation in deep learning segmentation, we can improve the accuracy and reliability of downstream analysis, such as cell counting, morphology analysis, and disease diagnosis.

This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation from ultra-high-resolution images. Using a locality-aware contextual correlation, we obtain accurate and efficient segmentation. By comparing our method with other existing methods, we show that our method has a high ability to accurately identify objects in complex backgrounds, while maintaining a fast processing speed. This study reveals a potential of new image processing techniques by learning from the locality-aware context correlation to improve the accuracy and speed of the ultra-high-resolution image processing.

Model Predictive Control (MPC) is widely used control strategy for nonlinear systems. In this paper, we apply MPC to a coupled tank liquid level system, which consists of two tanks connected by a pipe. The system is modeled using set of differential equations that describe flow of liquid between the tanks. The MPC algorithm is used to control the system by predicting future behavior of system and adjusting control inputs accordingly. The performance of the MPC algorithm is evaluated using simulation studies and compared to other control strategies. The results show that MPC is effective in controlling the system and can improve the stability and performance of system.

In this paper, we continue our study of M-theory compactifications on foliated backgrounds, building upon the base provided in the first publication. We investigate further concepts in M-theory: exceptional generalised geometry, foliations and their interaction to provide a broader understanding and scope of M-theory compactification. We delve deeper into novel solutions allowing for non-trivial foliations in M-theory and explore the tension between constraints on the geometry set by supersymmetry and compactness. In concluding, we also touch on the implications of our research on supergravity solutions and propose directions for subsequent studies.

Our work follows earlier work to recover topological information about image representations in deep networks and other architectures (Savage et al., 2012; Lidz et al., 2013). To gain insights into the Underlying architecture, our methods can be Directly used on real images, allowing one to test the generality of our proposed model. For Example, our algorithm recovers the feature space of an arbitrary fMRI image of interest perfectly even when there are no regions with higher than 90%, 95% Or 99% signal. Thus, our method provides both robustness against loss due to limited training data size as well as superior performance when Not constrained by sparse feature maps.

We propose a new residual-sparse fuzzy $C$-means clustering method based on wavelet frames. The new method combines the strength of fuzzy $C$-means and sparse clustering in a product quantization framework, where sparse clustering is used to identify prominent features of data, and fuzzy $C$-means is used to cluster data in the prominent features' space while considering the noise as residuals. We solve the minimization problem of our proposed method efficiently using morphological reconstruction and wavelet frames. In particular, we exploit the multi-resolution analysis property of wavelet frames to adaptively select the important features at different scales, and Morphological Reconstruction to effectively suppress the noise. The proposed method is evaluated on synthetic data and real-world image data, and results demonstrate effectiveness of new approach.

We give a general approach for computing second extensions between modules of graded Hecke algebras using a graded version of the second extension group. We therefore provide a technique for computing first extensions between modules of graded Hecke algebra using the graded version of the first extension group.

We propose a method for constructing a non-negative low-rank and sparse graph using data-adaptive features. Our method leverages a robust optimisation framework to capture the underlying structure in a given dataset. We begin by constructing a skeletonne graph using a non-negative least squares algorithm. This initial graph is then iteratively refined using a graph sparsification technique and a low-rank approximation. The resulting graph is a non-negative low-rank and sparse representation of the data that captures the underlying patterns and relationships. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of datasets, including synthetic data and real-world datasets. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of graph quality and running time.

This paper presents a comprehensive study on Minkowski measurability criteria for compact sets and relative fractal drums in Euclidean spaces. The research delves into the mathematical intricacies of Minkowski content and its measurability, providing a detailed analysis of the conditions under which a compact set in Euclidean space is Minkowski measurable. The paper also explores the concept of relative fractal drums, extending the theory of Minkowski measurability to these structures. The results provide a deeper understanding of the geometric and topological properties of compact sets and fractal drums, contributing to the broader field of fractal geometry.

The purpose  of  this paper  is  to implement  an image  segmentation approach based on   least absolute deviation fit. The proposed method includes fitting  a two-dimensional Gaussian or L1 distribution, including  the mean and  variance as well as  intercepts with  standard deviations of 5 degrees for the fitted  values. Our results demonstrate that this particular  model significantly outperforms other classification algorithms such as logistic regression and neural  networks (e.g., C4.0) and it can be applied in various nonimage  recognition tasks such as scene reconstruction because of it's excellent performance against traditional image segmentation methods  such as K-means, linear regression,  SVM or boosting.

In this paper, we consider the problem of determining the length of an s-increasing sequence of r-tuples. An s-increasing sequence of r-tuples is a sequence of r-tuples in which each element is obtained by adding a fixed positive integer vector to the previous element. We show that the length of such a sequence is at most exponential in the dimension of the vector space spanned by the sequence, and that this bound is tight. We also provide a characterisation of the cases in which the bound is achieved, and discuss the implications of our results for related problems in combinatorial mathematics. Our results have applications in the study of combinatorial objects such as compositions and partitions, and in the analysis of algorithms for solving problems in these areas.

The proposed  method automatically groups pixels in an image into clusters based on  their  similarity, with potential applications in  areas such as  image segmentation and object recognition. Experimental results demonstrate that the MW-based method outperforms traditional approaches while requiring significantly  less computational  resources. Overall, this  study provides  valuable insights into how bioinspired  algorithms can  be  leveraged to enhance computer vision techniques.

The finite element formulation of general boundary conditions for incompressible flows is presented in this paper. The formulation allows for the accurate representation of complex boundaries and flow conditions. The numerical solution is obtained using a Galerkin approach, and the stability and accuracy of the method are discussed. The paper includes detailed examples of the application of the method to various flow problems, demonstrating its ability to handle a wide range of boundary conditions and flow configurations.

The Holistic Decomposition Convolution (HDC) method is a novel approach to semantic segmentation of three-dimensional magnetic resonance (3D MR) images. This technique utilizes convolutional neural networks and incorporates holistic decomposition, which allows for more effective feature extraction and improved accuracy in image classification. The HDC model was trained on a large dataset of 3D MR images and demonstrated superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art methods in segmenting various anatomical structures within the brain. Overall, this study highlights the potential of the HDC method as a powerful tool for automated analysis of complex medical imaging data.

W-Net is a novel deep learning model proposed for fully unsupervised image segmentation. The proposed approach employs three levels of encoder networks to learn low, mid and high level representations of images and then uses these representations along with self-attention mechanisms to generate pixel-wise masks for each object within an image. Unlike existing methods that rely on labeled training data or supervision, W-Net can automatically detect objects in images without requiring any prior knowledge of their labels or locations. Our experiments show that W-Net outperforms state-of-the-art models on commonly used benchmark datasets including PASCAL VOC 2012. Furthermore, we demonstrate effectiveness of our model by qualitatively analyzing generated masks to understand how it is able to infer object boundaries from raw input images. Overall, our work contributes significantly to advancing field of image segmentation and opens up opportunities for new applications in various domains such as autonomous driving and medical imaging.

This research provides a novel margin preserving self-paced contrastive learning methodology towards domain adaptation for medical image segmentation. The proposed approach seeks to address the challenge of developing models trained on one dataset to perform well on another, especially in situations where there is limited labeled data available in the target domain. By integrating both self-paced learning and contrastive loss functions into our methodology, we are able to quickly reduce the effect of noisy samples while maintaining feature alignment between source and target domains. Through numerous studies utilizing publicly accessible databases, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy over different clinical imaging techniques. Overall, this work demonstrates an effective solution for identifying the issue of domain adaptation in clinical image analysis, with potential applications in other medical settings.

Semi-supervised medical image segmentation is a critical task in producing accurate labels for limited training data. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware multi-view co-learning approach to reduce the performance on unseen images with low supervision. Our method uses several auxiliary sources of knowledge (e.g., spatial accuracy and interpreter confidence) using the adversarial learning methodology to improve label generation in areas that are challenging with regard to the label reliability. We therefore incorporate domain adaptation into our model to accommodate imaging techniques beyond the initial source domain.

Our proposed approach uses three objective functions: one minimizing supervised loss and another eliminating self-correlation, which measures how close each predicted mask closely approximates its neighbor masks as defined by their similarity metrics. The supervised loss encourages correct classification while the self-correlation encourages additional confidence in overlapping masks. Also, we introduce attention mechanism to guide the focus on informative areas during training.

We demonstrate the validity of our method through multiple benchmarks by combining it with two state-of-the-art deep networks on multiple clinical datasets including heart, chest x ray, and cancer with differing levels of supervisions. Our findings show that domain adaptation can greatly improve the model's accuracy against unseen classes while not increasing the reliability in situations where fine-tuning labeled data involves minimal cost or time.

Overall, our methodology creates a very flexible manner to leverage uncertainty to produce predictions more efficiently, even when supervision is limited while allowing generalization over many domains with significant re-training efforts.

In this paper, we propose a new perspective on medical segmentation with uncertainty. We formulate problem as learning task in which a model is trained to predict segmentation mask with associated uncertainty map. The uncertainty map encodes model's confidence in its predictions and can be used to identify regions of the image where the segmentation is more uncertain. We evaluate our approach on two medical image segmentation tasks: liver segmentation and tumor segmentation. We find that our approach outperforms existing methods on both tasks, and that predicted uncertainty maps are effective at identifying regions of the image where the segmentation is more uncertain.

In this paper, we present a new loss function - the Lovasz-softmax loss - that enables neural models to optimize efficiently the intersection-over-union (IoU) or Jaccard similarity between their outputs and ground truth predictions. This is an important problem in machine learning, as IoU measures the degree of overlap between two sets (e.g., object detection vs object segmentation). While there are effective existing techniques for measuring such overlap (e.g., bounding box methods), these are generally computationally expensive or ad hoc to different tasks. We propose a tractable surrogate to IOU based on the Hungarian algorithm, which can be used directly with popular optimization methods like stochastic gradient descent. Moreover, we analyze its properties theoretically, showing that it retains key insights from recent work while being much more efficient to evaluate and update. To demonstrate our approach, we apply it to several benchmark datasets, including image classification, semantic segmentation, and instance segmentation. Our experiments show that our proposed method achieves competitive results over state-of-the-art counterparts while significantly reducing computational cost.

The Hierarchical Cont-Bouchaud model is a novel approach to understanding the behavior of complex systems, particularly those with multiple levels of organization. 

This model combines the Cont-Bouchaud model, which is a well-established statistical physics model for disordered systems, with a hierarchical structure that allows for the analysis of systems with multiple levels of organization. The model is based on the idea that complex systems can be broken down into smaller, simpler subsystems that interact with each other in a hierarchical manner. These subsystems are modeled using the Cont-Bouchaud model, which takes into account the interactions between particles in a disordered system. Previous works have demonstrated that deep neural networks (DNNs) can develop meaningful shape representations. Unfortunately, existing techniques need considerable training and suffer from the dataset imbalance problem, i.e., the scarcity of labeled items with regard to the background. In this paper, we present a basic yet effective method for object discovery through cohesion measurement. Given a group of points in the 3D space, our approach can automatically discover the objects with coherent structures. We propose a novel cohesion measurement by examining the intrinsic interaction between points, which captures the object boundaries in a learnable way. In this paper, we propose a novel visual saliency model based on multiscale deep features. The proposed model is composed of two parts: a deep feature extraction part and a saliency prediction part. The saliency prediction part is based on the multiscale deep features extracted from the deep feature extraction part. The saliency prediction part is composed of two parts: a multiscale deep feature fusion part and a saliency prediction part. The multiscale deep feature fusion part is used to fuse the multiscale deep features extracted from the deep feature extraction part. The saliency prediction part is used to predict the saliency map from the fused multiscale deep features. The proposed model is evaluated on the MIT-SALIENCY dataset and the ECSSD dataset. The experimental results show that the proposed model outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

In this paper, we explore the Gaussian core model in high dimensions, a topic of great interest and relevance in various fields such as machine learning, signal processing, and statistics. The Gaussian core model is a popular probabilistic model used to represent data with a large number of features or variables, and it has been widely applied in various domains including image and text analysis. However, the traditional Gaussian core model is limited to low-dimensional settings, and its extension to high-dimensional spaces remains an open challenge.

In this work, we propose a novel approach to extend the Gaussian core model to high-dimensional spaces, leverageing recent advances in random matrix theory and probability theory. Our proposed method enables the estimation of the parametres of the Gaussian core model in high dimensions, allowing for more accurate representation and analysis of complex data sets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive simulations and real-data experiments, showcasing its ability to outperform existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

Our main contributions can be summarised as follows:

* We introduce a novel approach to extend the Gaussian core model to high-dimensional spaces, which enables the estimation of the model parametres using maxeimum likelihood estimation.
* We derive the closed-form expression of the log-likelihood function of the extended Gaussian core model, which facilitates efficient optimisation algorithms for parametre estimation.

This paper provides valuable insights into the application of the Gaussian core model in high-dimensional spaces, and offers a powerful tool for analysing and modelling complex data sets in various fields.

With its  rapid progress,  AI has quickly evolved into an important area in medical diagnostics. We propose a  deep neural network  architecture optimized by using the learned feature representations given in past training  data  to estimate the presence of atria recurrence during outflow or arrest phases along   with time  lapse between  successive arrests. The model features are trained on  3-D digital  versions of atria. In conclusion, our technique  provides a solution to problems associated  with high cost and poor predictability of treatment decision during cardiac arrest during end-of-life  hospitalization; namely the late  arrival on trial of post-discharge ARFs, long  delays before recovery of heart functions after  return stroke,  and high risk of severe  left ventricular dysfunction after discharge.

Deep neural networks were shown to perform successfully on large scale biomedical image segmentation task, such as ISBI, but struggled when used in real environments like hospitals due to distribution shift issue between training and testing images caused by different physical environment (e.g. lighting conditions), data acquisition technique (e.g., detector's resolution or viewpoint) ,and patient characteristic (such as weight). To handle this challenge, we propose unsupervised cross modality domain adaptation of convolutional neural network (CNN) for biomedical image segmentations and use adversarial learning to match features across modalities without accessing ground truth labels. Experiments show that our method achieves significant improvement compared to prior art while reducing requirement of groundtruth annotations.

> Cardiovascular disease is one of the biggest health problems worldwide.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is widely used for non-invasive detection of myocardial abnormalities. Cardiac MRI images can be characterized by different modalities. Cardiac MRI images, consisting of multiple long axis planes, represent one of the imaging challenges. 

The presence of long axis planes requires effective solutions for segmenting the myocardium. This paper uses 2D and 3D deep neural networks to segment the myocardium from cardiac MRI images. We developed a 3D dilated convolution network (3DDCN) and a 3D gated convolution network (3DGCN). The proposed models use 3D convolution, with a set of techniques to handle the data structure. 

We evaluated different techniques to generate effective 3D representations.

We investigate effective methods to incorporate local and global features. 

Overall, the proposed methods represent effective techniques to handle data in 2D and 3D. The proposed 3D deep learning models can handle the long axis planes in cardiac MRI images. In addition, the proposed methods represent an effective solution for integrating data from the long axis planes.

This academic paper introduces a novel approach to enhance semantic Image segmentation using near-infrared information. Traditional methods for semantic image segmentation rely Solely on visible light, which limits their ability to accurately identify objects in low light or challenging conditions. In this paper, we propose a method that combines visible light images with near-infrared images to improve segmentation accuracy. We utilize a deep neural network architecture that takes advantage of the Complementary information provided by near-infrared images. Experimental Results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms Traditional methods in challenging lighting conditions. This research has important implications for various applications, including autonomous driving, surveillance, and medical imaging.

Edge-set graphs are graph structures that Have edges in all directions, and which can be represented by a set of vertices (or nodes) connected to each other by edges. The edge-set structure allows us to represent graphs with arbitrary number of vertices, and It also enables us to efficiently compute the shortest path between two vertices. In this work we present an algorithm for computing the shortest path between Two vertices Using edge-set Graphs. We show That our algorithm is faster than the fastest known algorithms for such computations, and that it achieves comparable performance when compared to the best known algorithms for these problems. Our results demonstrate that edge-set graphs provide a new way to solve graph search problems.

The sensor location problem is a fundamental issue in wireless sensor networks (WSNs) that aims to determine the optimal locations for a set of sensors to monitor a given area. This paper presents an extensive study on the characteristics of optimal solutions to the sensor location problem. We first review the different approaches and metrics used to solve this problem, including minimum variance, maxeimum coverage, and entropy-based methods. Then, we analyse the performance of these algorithms using simulation studies and real-world examples. Our results show that the choice of metric depends on the specific application requirements and environment conditions. Furthermore, we identify some common patterns and trends in the optimal solution characteristics across different scenarios. These include the importance of density and clustreing in sensor deployment, the impact of obstacles and terrain on sensing coverage, and the trade-off between communication and sensing costs. Finally, we discuss some open issues and future directions for research in this field, including the integration of multiple objectives and constraints, the use of machine learning techniques for optimisation, and the development of more efficient algorithms for large-scale WSNs.

Human error and human perception are often confused, but they are not the same thing. In this work we study how people perceive images with different levels of detail (e.g. low-resolution, high-resolution) and how this perception can be used to infer the level of human error in the processing of medical images. We demonstrate that people do indeed have a very good intuitive understanding of the quality of an image, even for low-resolution images. However, our results show that human perception may also contain errors. In particular, we show that people overestimate the amount of human error in the segmentation of high-resolution images compared to low-resolution images. This effect was even more pronounced for images with more detail. Our results provide evidence that people use visual information about the surface details of an object to judge the overall quality of the image.
